newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government gets mixed news on strikes.
newsitem.headline: French government gets mixed news on strikes.

text.p: A week-old French industrial dispute at oil giant Elf Aquitaine deepened on Thursday, although Prime Minister Alain Juppe's strike-weary government received slight relief when airline pilots called off a stoppage.

In industrial action partly inspired by concessions won last week by truckers as a result of a 12-day blockade, workers also pursued local transport strikes in two major cities and urged new protests at post offices and defence-related firms.
After talks to try to end a refinery strike over 330 job cuts at Elf, which went into its eighth day on Thursday, union leaders said management proposals were unacceptable.
Unions slammed the Elf offer of more pay and earlier retirement as irrelevant to their main concern over jobs.
However an Elf spokesman described the four-hour negotiating session as having gone well and said the company had made proposals which unions would put to their members.
Elf has said the job reductions are necessary to meet fierce competition and cannot be negotiated.

France's largest union, the Socialist CFDT, recommended the refinery strike go on while the Communist-backed CGT union took a slightly softer line, saying it was up to strikers to decide whether to go back to work on the strength of what it called "insufficient" proposals.
Unions said Elf had offered a 1.5 percent pay increase and a cut in retirement age for shift workers to 56 or 57, depending on seniority. But unions wanted planned job cuts scrapped first.
Unions now hope to spread disruption across the French oil industry with a nationwide strike on December 10.

In one piece of good news for management negotiators, a spokesman for the airline pilots' union said a two-day strike slated for December 10-11 had been called off. This followed signs of a possible breakthrough in a long-running labour conflict on job contracts.
In other disputes, striking bus drivers paralysed services in the southern city of Toulouse for the third day on Thursday over early retirement.

Public transport in Lyon, France's second city, was reduced in a protest over recent assaults on bus drivers, but a resumption of service appeared near after driver unions and management reached agreement on their differences, union officials said late on Thursday.
Meanwhile, the CGT union canvassed support for a week of action at post offices from December 9 to protest against partial privatisation plans.
The CGT also urged employees of French defence firms to step up protests December 9-20 against government restructuring plans in the defence sector.
France's truck drivers, whose strike ended on Friday, gained a cut in the retirement age to 55 from 60 for drivers with 25 years' experience.
The Elf strike has caused a huge logistical problem for Elf and helped to drive up international gasoline prices.
Oil traders said it had been forced to buy 100,000 tonnes of petrol on the open market and divert or sell tonnes of crude.
But the strike's impact has been slow to get through to ordinary consumers, in part because of the blockade of depots by the French truckers last month, which kept most tanks full.
